1. Market Overview & Long-Term Price Trend

Gold has undergone three distinct structural phases over the 25-year sample:

  • 2000–2008 (Base Building): Gold traded in a relatively narrow range (~$270–$1,000), oscillating with low趋势 visibility. The early years (2000–2003) show flat OHLC bars consistent with London PM fix pricing rather than continuous market data.
  • 2008–2011 (Bull Run): Following the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, gold surged from ~$800 to a then-ATH of ~$1,900 in 2011 — a near-2.5× appreciation driven by monetary easing, sovereign debt concerns, and safe-haven flows.
  • 2011–2025 (Structural Broader Upward Channel): After a correction to ~$1,050 in 2015–16, gold entered a sustained multi-year rally. The breakout above $2,000 in 2020 (COVID) and subsequent move to multi-thousand-dollar levels ($5,000+) by 2025 reflects a fundamental repricing of the metal amid fiscal deficits, de-dollarization trends, and geopolitical risk.
Key Inflection Points:
• Aug 2000: $273.90 (dataset open) → Dec 2015 low: $1050.80
• Sep 2011 ATH: $5377.30 on 2026-03-03
• 2025 peak so far: $5377.30 as of 2026-03-03

2. Volatility Analysis & Regime Detection

Volatility in gold is highly regime-dependent. Using a 63-day rolling window (~one trading quarter), we classify each observation into Low (<10% annualized), Medium (10–20%), or High (>20%) volatility regimes.

3. Seasonal & Calendar-Based Patterns

To assess whether gold exhibits recurring seasonal patterns, we compute mean daily log returns by month and day-of-week, and test whether observed differences are statistically distinguishable from zero using a t-test. Bars marked with * indicate p-value < 0.10.

Fig 6. Left: distribution of daily log returns by month (boxplot). Right: mean daily return by month with statistical significance markers. Observed variation is small relative to daily volatility.

4. Return Distribution & Tail Risk

Gold's daily return distribution deviates meaningfully from normality, exhibiting fat tails and, to a lesser extent, negative skew. This has direct implications for VaR/CVaR estimates and risk model choice.

Fig 8. Left: histogram of daily log returns with normal overlay. The excess kurtosis is visually apparent in the peaked center and fat tails. Right: Q-Q plot — departure from the diagonal line confirms non-normality, particularly in the tails.

6. Key Takeaways & Forward-Looking Considerations

1. Volatility is Regimestructured, Not Constant
Gold spends ~82% of the time in low-to-medium volatility regimes. High-vol crises are episodic — typically coinciding with systemic financial events (2008, 2020, 2022). Risk models should use regime-switching or GARCH approaches rather than constant-vol assumptions.
2. The Sharpe-Like Ratio of 0.70 is Attractive on a Risk-Adjusted Basis
With CAGR of 12.4% and annualized volatility of 17.7%, gold's risk-adjusted return profile compares favorably to many fixed-income and equity benchmarks over the same period. However, this is backward-looking; forward Sharpe ratios depend on the regime.
3. Maximum Drawdown of -48.4% is a Tail Risk Reality
Even in a predominantly upward-trending asset, intermediate drawdowns can be severe. Historical drawdowns exceeding 30% (2008–09, 2011–15) show that gold can suffer multi-year negative periods, particularly when real rates rise or the USD strengthens.
4. No Reliable Seasonal Edge
The seasonal analysis shows no statistically significant monthly or weekday effect in gold returns. While February appears marginally stronger, the p-values are well above significance thresholds. Seasonal strategies based on calendar effects in gold are not supported by this data.
5. Fat Tails Require Robust Risk Models
The excess kurtosis of 7.02 and negative skew confirm that gold returns have heavier tails than a normal distribution. Standard parametric VaR understates tail risk. Use historical simulation or fat-tailed distributions for risk estimation.
6. Current Context (as of March 2026)
With gold at $5377.30, the current vol regime is High. Recent momentum (60-day ROC: 28.1%) is positive. Analysts should monitor real rate dynamics, central bank buying, and geopolitical risk as primary regime drivers.
